appeal_from: Court of Appeal (England and Wales) [2025] EWCA Civ 658, [2025] ICR 1404, on appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal [2024] EAT 117
facts: The Appellant (the Driver) worked as an employee for the Respondent (the Operator), a small private hire business, in 2016. He worked on average 34.8 hours a week. The tribunal found that drivers generally averaged over 43 hours a week, some 60 or more, and so treated him as a part-time worker. His chosen comparator averaged over 90 hours a week, which the tribunal did not find inappropriate. All drivers, full-time or part-time, paid the same fixed weekly fee (GBP 148) for access to the Operator's booking and dispatch system, irrespective of hours worked. The Driver therefore paid more per hour than his comparator and took home less per hour. He claimed under regulation 5 of the Part-Time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000 that this was less favourable treatment on the ground that he was a part-time worker. The Operator did not seek to justify any such treatment on objective grounds. The employment tribunal dismissed the claim. Its primary finding was that treating all drivers alike was not less favourable treatment. Alternatively, it found that the fee was charged to generate revenue for the business, which was how private hire firms operated, and that the Operator may then have lacked software allowing a commission-based system. It held that any differential impact was therefore not on the sole ground that he was a part-time worker, following McMenemy v Capita Business Services Ltd [2007] CSIH 25, a decision of the Inner House of the Court of Session. The Employment Appeal Tribunal held that there was less favourable treatment once the pro rata principle was applied, and that this part of the tribunal's reasoning was wrong. It nevertheless dismissed the appeal, considering itself bound by McMenemy on the causation question, and gave permission to appeal. The Court of Appeal (Bean, Edis and Elisabeth Laing LJJ) also dismissed the appeal, by a majority, applying McMenemy and the requirement that part-time status be the sole ground. The Court of Appeal gave permission to appeal to the Supreme Court so that the causation question could be resolved for the whole United Kingdom. The Driver appeals.

issues.question: Does the right in regulation 5(1) of the Part-Time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000 apply only where part-time status is the sole ground of the less favourable treatment, such that it is not enough that part-time status is an effective cause of it?

appellant_submissions: The words "on the ground that" in regulation 5(2)(a) have a settled meaning in discrimination law. The protected characteristic need only be an effective or substantial cause of the treatment, and need not be the sole or main cause. Examples are Nagarajan v London Regional Transport [2000] 1 AC 501, O'Neill v Governors of St Thomas More School, and later whistleblowing detriment cases such as Fecitt v NHS Manchester. The Regulations do not contain the words "solely" or "sole". Section 19(1) of the Employment Relations Act 1999 is a wide enabling power, and the Regulations could lawfully give wider protection than clause 4.1 of the Framework Agreement. The Secretary of State chose established domestic language rather than copying "solely because". Even if the Regulations are read consistently with the Directive, the case law of the CJEU has never analysed "solely" as excluding cases with more than one cause. Cases such as MK v Lufthansa CityLine and Lalfi treated other reasons as matters of objective justification. The purpose of the Framework Agreement is to eliminate discrimination against part-time workers and the protection should not be read restrictively. A sole-cause test produces arbitrary results, as in Sharma v Manchester City Council, where an employer could escape liability by adding a second criterion. Other causes are relevant to justification and to compensation.
respondent_submissions: The 2000 Regulations were made to implement the Part-time Work Directive and should be read consistently with clause 4.1 of the Framework Agreement, which prohibits less favourable treatment "solely because" a worker works part time. The CJEU has repeatedly stated clause 4.1 in terms of the "sole ground" (Wippel and later cases). The word "only" and the singular "ground" in regulation 5(2), contrasted with the different formulations in regulations 6 and 7, point to a single-cause test. The Regulations are carefully limited. They cover direct discrimination only, require an actual comparator and allow objective justification, so the sole-cause test fits that scheme. The Framework Agreement was a negotiated compromise on a contentious subject, and it differs deliberately from wider equality instruments that use different wording. McMenemy correctly adopted the sole-ground test and both courts below treated it as binding. Here the fee was charged to generate revenue, as is standard in the industry, and the Operator's software may not have permitted another approach. Part-time status was therefore not the sole ground. The Regulations should be read in line with the Directive unless Parliament clearly signalled a wider test, and no such signal appears.
legal_materials: Regulation 5 of the Part-Time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000: (1) a part-time worker has the right not to be treated less favourably than a comparable full-time worker as regards the terms of the contract or by any other detriment; (2) the right applies "only if (a) the treatment is on the ground that the worker is a part-time worker, and (b) the treatment is not justified on objective grounds"; (3) the pro rata principle applies unless inappropriate. Regulations 6, 7 and 8(6) (reasons for treatment; "the reason (or, if more than one, the principal reason)"; employer to identify the ground). Section 19 of the Employment Relations Act 1999 (wide power to secure that part-time employees are treated no less favourably; also to comply with the Directive). Clause 4.1 of the Framework Agreement annexed to Directive 97/81/EC: part-time workers shall not be treated less favourably "solely because they work part time unless different treatment is justified on objective grounds"; clause 6.1 (more favourable provisions permitted). Authorities: Nagarajan; O'Neill; Fecitt; Wippel (C-313/02); MK v Lufthansa CityLine (C-660/20); Lalfi (C-268/24); McMenemy; Sharma; United States v Nolan [2015] UKSC 63.
actual_reasoning_summary: The Supreme Court held that regulation 5(2)(a) is satisfied where part-time status is an effective cause of the less favourable treatment, and that it need not be the sole cause. The phrase "on the ground that" had a well-established meaning in discrimination law by 2000, covering significant or effective causes and not only sole ones. The Court found it unnecessary to decide what "solely because" means in clause 4.1, because no conforming construction was required. Section 19 of the 1999 Act and clause 6.1 allowed the Regulations to give wider protection than the Directive, and the Secretary of State chose established domestic wording instead of "solely". The word "only" in regulation 5(2) qualifies both conditions and does not set a causation test, and the singular "ground" refers to the single protected status. A sole-cause test would produce unreasonable outcomes, and other causes are relevant to objective justification and compensation. McMenemy was wrongly decided on this point and the Court of Appeal's contrary approach was in error.
outcome_evidence: Para 87: "For these reasons (which are essentially the same as those given by the Court of Appeal majority), I would allow the appeal. The 2000 Regulations prohibit less favourable treatment of part-time workers where their part-time status is an effective cause of the impugned treatment. It need not be the sole cause." Lady Simler gave the judgment, with whom Lord Lloyd-Jones, Lord Hamblen, Lord Leggatt and Lord Richards agreed (header, para 10).
